lesson_scope: Proving quadratic expressions are strictly positive or non-negative using completed square form, finding parameter bounds for strictly positive/negative expressions, connecting completed-square form to minimum/maximum values, and proving non-intersection of lines and curves via completed-square difference without real roots.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: reading minimum value from a completed square form and explaining strict positivity.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of reading minimum value from vertex form and proving positivity.

hints: Recall that the square of any real number is non-negative: $(x - 4)^2 \ge 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.
The minimum value of $(x - 4)^2$ is $0$, which occurs when $x = 4$.
Therefore, the minimum value of $(x - 4)^2 + 7$ is $0 + 7 = 7$. Since $7 > 0$, the expression is always strictly positive.

walkthrough.text:
Consider the properties of the squared term for any real number $x$:
$$(x - 4)^2 \ge 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{R}$$

Find the minimum value, which occurs when the squared bracket equals zero ($x = 4$):
$$\text{Minimum value} = 0 + 7 = 7$$

Conclude the positivity proof:
$$\text{Since } (x - 4)^2 + 7 \ge 7 \text{ and } 7 > 0, \text{ the expression is strictly positive for all real } x.$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: completing the square on a monic quadratic to find the parameter range for strict positivity.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of setting minimum value > 0 to ensure an expression is always positive.

hints: Complete the square for the quadratic: $x^2 + 8x + k = (x + 4)^2 - 16 + k$.
For the expression to be strictly positive for all real $x$, the minimum value must be strictly greater than $0$: $k - 16 > 0 \implies k > 16$.

walkthrough.text:
Complete the square for $x^2 + 8x + k$:
$$x^2 + 8x + k = (x + 4)^2 - 4^2 + k = (x + 4)^2 + (k - 16)$$

Identify the minimum value of the expression, which occurs at $x = -4$:
$$\text{Minimum value} = k - 16$$

Set the condition for the expression to be strictly positive for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$:
$$k - 16 > 0 \implies k > 16$$

ai_rubric.observable: Completes the square to obtain $(x + 4)^2 + k - 16$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: completing the square for a non-monic quadratic and finding its minimum value.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of completing the square for a > 1 to extract the minimum value.

hints: Factor out $2$ from the first two terms: $2(x^2 - 6x) + 23$.
Complete the square inside the bracket: $x^2 - 6x = (x - 3)^2 - 9$.
Since $2(x - 3)^2 \ge 0$, the minimum value is $+5$ (occurring at $x = 3$).

walkthrough.text:
Identify the parameters $p$ and $q$:
$$p = 3 \quad \text{and} \quad q = 5$$

State the minimum value of the quadratic function:
$$\text{Since } 2(x - 3)^2 \ge 0, \text{ the minimum value is } 5 \text{ (occurring at } x = 3\text{).}$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: determining the parameter range for an inverted quadratic expression to remain strictly negative.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of bounding maximum value < 0 for negative quadratic forms.

hints: Because $-(x + 5)^2 \le 0$, the maximum possible value of the expression is $10 - k$ (at $x = -5$).
For the expression to be strictly negative ($< 0$) for all real $x$, its maximum value must be less than $0$: $10 - k < 0 \implies k > 10$.

walkthrough.text:
Group the constant terms to identify the vertex / maximum value:
$$E(x) = (10 - k) - (x + 5)^2$$

Since $-(x + 5)^2 \le 0$ for all real $x$, the maximum value of $E(x)$ is:
$$\text{Maximum value} = 10 - k$$

Require the maximum value to be strictly negative for $E(x) < 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$:
$$10 - k < 0 \implies k > 10$$

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies the maximum value as $10 - k$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: proving algebraically by completing the square that a quadratic equation has no real roots.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of proving non-existence of real roots via completing the square.

hints: Explain that because $(x + 2)^2 \ge 0$ for all real $x$, it cannot equal $-5$, so no real solutions exist.

walkthrough.text:
Complete the square for the quadratic equation:
$$x^2 + 4x + 9 = 0$$
$$(x + 2)^2 - 2^2 + 9 = 0$$
$$(x + 2)^2 + 5 = 0$$

Rearrange to isolate the squared bracket:
$$(x + 2)^2 = -5$$

State the contradiction for real $x$:
$$\text{For all } x \in \mathbb{R}, \quad (x + 2)^2 \ge 0.$$
$$\text{Since } (x + 2)^2 \ge 0 > -5, \text{ there are no real solutions.}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Concludes that no real solutions exist because a real square cannot be negative.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: proving non-intersection of a straight line and a parabola using completed-square form.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of proving curve and line do not intersect using completed square.

hints: Equate the curve and line equations: $x^2 + 5 = 2x + 2$.
Complete the square: $(x - 1)^2 + 2 = 0 \implies $(x - 1)^2 = -2$, which is impossible for real $x$, so no intersection points exist.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the two equations to find the $x$-coordinates of any intersection points:
$$x^2 + 5 = 2x + 2$$
$$x^2 - 2x + 3 = 0$$

Complete the square for the resulting quadratic:
$$(x - 1)^2 - 1^2 + 3 = 0$$
$$(x - 1)^2 + 2 = 0 \implies (x - 1)^2 = -2$$

Conclude that no real intersection points exist:
$$\text{Since } (x - 1)^2 \ge 0 \text{ for all } x \in \mathbb{R}, (x - 1)^2 \text{ cannot equal } -2.$$
$$\text{Therefore, the curve and the line do not intersect.}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Forms $x^2 - 2x + 3 = 0$ and completes the square to get $(x - 1)^2 = -2$.
Concludes that the line and curve do not intersect since $(x - 1)^2 \ge 0$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Easy: finding a parameter range for a monic quadratic to be strictly positive for all real x.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires completing the square to establish strict positivity conditions on a parameter.

hints: Identify the minimum value of this upward-opening parabola, which is $p - 25$.
For the expression to be strictly positive for all real $x$, set $\text{minimum value} > 0$.

walkthrough.text:
Complete the square for $x^2 - 10x + p$:
$$x^2 - 10x + p = (x - 5)^2 - 5^2 + p = (x - 5)^2 + (p - 25)$$
Since $(x - 5)^2 \ge 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the minimum value of the expression is $p - 25$.

For the expression to be strictly positive ($> 0$) for all real $x$, the minimum value must be strictly positive:
$$p - 25 > 0 \implies p > 25$$

ai_rubric.observable: Completes the square to obtain $(x - 5)^2 - 25 + p$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Easy: using completing the square to prove a numerical minimum bound and identifying the point of equality.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Proves global minimum bound via vertex form and extracts minimum location.

hints: Use the property that any real square is non-negative: $(x + 3)^2 \ge 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

walkthrough.text:
Apply the property that the square of a real number is always non-negative:
$$(x + 3)^2 \ge 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{R}$$
$$(x + 3)^2 + 5 \ge 5 \implies x^2 + 6x + 14 \ge 5$$

Find the value of $x$ where equality holds:
$$(x + 3)^2 = 0 \implies x + 3 = 0 \implies x = -3$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: completing the square with leading coefficient 3 and determining parameter values for a lower function bound.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires non-monic completing the square with parametric constant term.

hints: Factor out $3$ from the first two terms: $3(x^2 + 4x) + c$.
Complete the square inside the bracket: $x^2 + 4x = (x + 2)^2 - 4$.

walkthrough.text:
Factor out $3$ from the $x$-terms:
$$3x^2 + 12x + c = 3(x^2 + 4x) + c$$

Complete the square inside the bracket:
$$= 3\left((x + 2)^2 - 4\right) + c = 3(x + 2)^2 - 12 + c = 3(x + 2)^2 + (c - 12)$$
$$\text{So } p = 2 \quad \text{and} \quad q = c - 12$$

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Deduces parameter inequality from non-zero function lower bound.

walkthrough.text: Since $3(x + 2)^2 \ge 0$ for all real $x$, the minimum value of $f(x)$ is $c - 12$.

For $f(x) > 2$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, set the minimum strictly greater than $2$:
$$c - 12 > 2 \implies c > 14$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: completing the square with a negative leading coefficient and bounding the maximum value to ensure strictly negative outputs.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires special completing the square into A - a(x-B)^2 form.

walkthrough.text:
Factor out $-2$ from the first two terms:
$$E(x) = -2(x^2 - 4x) - k$$

Complete the square inside the bracket:
$$= -2\left((x - 2)^2 - 4\right) - k = -2(x - 2)^2 + 8 - k = (8 - k) - 2(x - 2)^2$$
$$\text{So } B = 2 \quad \text{and} \quad A = 8 - k$$

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Deduces strictly negative condition from vertex maximum value.

hints: Notice that $-2(x - 2)^2 \le 0$, so the maximum value of $E(x)$ is $8 - k$.
For $E(x) < 0$ for all real $x$, the maximum value must be strictly negative.

walkthrough.text: Because $-2(x - 2)^2 \le 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the maximum value of $E(x)$ is $8 - k$ (occurring at $x = 2$).

For $E(x) < 0$ for all real $x$, the maximum value must be strictly negative:
$$8 - k < 0 \implies k > 8$$

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies the maximum value as $8 - k$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: proving non-intersection of curve and line by demonstrating a strictly positive completed-square difference.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Equates line and curve and completes the square.

walkthrough.text:
Set the $y$-values equal to find points of intersection:
$$x^2 - 4x + 9 = 2x + 1$$
$$x^2 - 6x + 8 = 0$$

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Proves non-intersection by showing difference equation has strictly positive minimum.

hints: Equate the curve to the new line: $x^2 - 4x + 9 = 2x - 5$.
Complete the square: $(x - 3)^2 + 5 = 0 \implies (x - 3)^2 = -5$, which is impossible for real $x$, proving no intersections.

walkthrough.text:
Equate the curve and the new line equation:
$$x^2 - 4x + 9 = 2x - 5$$
$$x^2 - 6x + 14 = 0$$
$$(x - 3)^2 - 9 + 14 = 0$$
$$(x - 3)^2 + 5 = 0$$

Since $(x - 3)^2 \ge 0$ for all real $x$, $(x - 3)^2 + 5 \ge 5 > 0$, so $(x - 3)^2 + 5 = 0$ has no real solutions.
$$\text{Hence the curve and the line } y = 2x - 5 \text{ do not intersect.}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Forms $x^2 - 6x + 14 = 0$ and completes the square to $(x - 3)^2 + 5 = 0$.
Explains that $(x - 3)^2 + 5 \ge 5 > 0$ means the equation has no real solutions.

questions.difficulty_reason: Hard: parametric completing the square with linear and quadratic parameter terms to ensure strictly positive expression.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Parametric completing the square with linear and quadratic k expressions.

hints: The coefficient of $x$ is $2(k - 1)$. Halving it gives $(k - 1)$, so the squared bracket is $(x + k - 1)^2$.
Simplify the constant terms: $-k^2 + 2k - 1 + k^2 - 3k + 7 = -k + 6 = 6 - k$. Thus $g(k) = 6 - k$.

walkthrough.text:
Complete the square on $x^2 + 2(k - 1)x$:
$$Q(x) = (x + (k - 1))^2 - (k - 1)^2 + (k^2 - 3k + 7)$$

Simplify like terms in $k$:
$$Q(x) = (x + k - 1)^2 + (-k^2 + k^2 + 2k - 3k - 1 + 7)$$
$$Q(x) = (x + k - 1)^2 + (6 - k)$$
$$\text{Thus } g(k) = 6 - k$$

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Solves parameter inequality from strictly positive vertex condition.

hints: The minimum value of $Q(x) = (x + k - 1)^2 + (6 - k)$ is $6 - k$.
For $Q(x) > 0$ for all real $x$, the minimum value must be strictly positive.

walkthrough.text: Since $(x + k - 1)^2 \ge 0$ for all real $x$, the minimum value of $Q(x)$ is $g(k) = 6 - k$.

For $Q(x) > 0$ for all real $x$, set the minimum value strictly greater than zero:
$$6 - k > 0 \implies k < 6$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Hard: algebraic completed-square proof with parametric leading coefficient and quadratic numerator inequality.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Parametric completing the square with rational fractional terms and target proof.

walkthrough.text:
Factor out $(m - 1)$ from the variable terms:
$$f(x) = (m - 1)\left(x^2 + \dfrac{6}{m - 1}x\right) + (m + 7)$$

Complete the square inside the bracket:
$$x^2 + \dfrac{6}{m - 1}x = \left(x + \dfrac{3}{m - 1}\right)^2 - \left(\dfrac{3}{m - 1}\right)^2 = \left(x + \dfrac{3}{m - 1}\right)^2 - \dfrac{9}{(m - 1)^2}$$

Distribute $(m - 1)$ and combine the constants over the common denominator $(m - 1)$:
$$f(x) = (m - 1)\left(x + \dfrac{3}{m - 1}\right)^2 - \dfrac{9}{m - 1} + (m + 7)$$
$$= (m - 1)\left(x + \dfrac{3}{m - 1}\right)^2 + \dfrac{(m + 7)(m - 1) - 9}{m - 1}$$
$$= (m - 1)\left(x + \dfrac{3}{m - 1}\right)^2 + \dfrac{m^2 + 6m - 7 - 9}{m - 1}$$
$$= (m - 1)\left(x + \dfrac{3}{m - 1}\right)^2 + \dfrac{m^2 + 6m - 16}{m - 1}$$
$$\text{Thus } R(m) = m^2 + 6m - 16$$

ai_rubric.observable: Expands numerator $(m + 7)(m - 1) - 9 = m^2 + 6m - 16$ to show $R(m) = m^2 + 6m - 16$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Deduces valid parameter range by solving quadratic numerator inequality.

hints: Since $m > 1$, the leading coefficient $(m - 1) > 0$, so the parabola opens upwards.
Factorise $(m + 8)(m - 2) > 0 \implies m < -8 \text{ or } m > 2$. Since $m > 1$, the only valid range is $m > 2$.

walkthrough.text:
Since $m > 1$, $(m - 1) > 0$, meaning the parabola opens upwards and has a true minimum value:
$$\text{Minimum value} = \dfrac{m^2 + 6m - 16}{m - 1}$$

Require the minimum value to be strictly positive:
$$\dfrac{m^2 + 6m - 16}{m - 1} > 0$$
$$\text{Since } m - 1 > 0, \quad m^2 + 6m - 16 > 0$$

Factorise the quadratic in $m$ and apply the domain restriction $m > 1$:
$$(m + 8)(m - 2) > 0 \implies m < -8 \quad \text{or} \quad m > 2$$
$$\text{Combining with } m > 1 \text{ gives the final solution set: } m > 2$$

ai_rubric.observable: Notes that $(m - 1) > 0$ and sets minimum value $\dfrac{m^2 + 6m - 16}{m - 1} > 0$.
